[PATH:theoretical] Integrated assessment models (e.g., IMAGE, GCAM) projecting material demand under digitalization and service-sector growth scenarios to 2040 — Simulates whether dematerialization and digital substitution can achieve 50% footprint reduction with sustained GDP growth, testing theoretical plausibility of the mechanism.

[PATH:empirical] Global carbon budget datasets (e.g., Global Carbon Project) combined with World Bank GDP data for all countries, not just OECD, to test if absolute decoupling extends beyond high-income economies. — The hypothesis claims projectability to global scale, but current evidence is limited to 32 OECD countries. Global data can confirm or refute whether decoupling rates are replicable in lower-income economies with technology transfer.

[PATH:empirical] Time-series analysis of sectoral emissions intensity and renewable energy penetration in emerging economies (e.g., China, India, Brazil) from 2005-2023 using IEA or IRENA data. — If absolute decoupling is accelerating globally, these high-emission, fast-growing economies should show declining emissions per unit GDP and increasing renewable shares. Failure to observe this would challenge the global extrapolation.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of technology diffusion and rebound effects (e.g., Jevons paradox literature) applied to renewable energy transitions. — The hypothesis assumes technology transfer leads to decoupling without accounting for potential rebound effects where efficiency gains increase overall resource use. A theoretical review can clarify whether the observed decoupling is sustainable or an artifact of short-term trends.

qualifier.detail: decoupling rates in leading economies exceed 3% annual emissions reduction while maintaining positive GDP growth, projectable to global scale through technology transfer
